DA03E17 was included as a positive control. Source data are provided as a Source Data file. c Cryo-EM maps of additional DR motif antibodies in complex with CA09 N1 sNAp, with overall resolutions ranging from 2.48 to 2.76 A. d Detailed interactions between the conserved DR motifs in the CDR H3 of additional DR motif antibodies and the NA active site residues. e Structural alignment of 8 DR motif antibodies by their bound NA protomer. The variable regions of the heavy and light chains (VH and VL) are colored in dark blue and light blue, respectively. f Cross-sectional view of the NA active site showing conserved DR motifs occupying the active site pocket.

To explore whether similar DR motif NA antibodies have been independently observed and to get a broader qualitative sense of their prevalence, we surveyed antibody sequences from patents and the literature for NA antibodies with a central DR motif in the CDR H3, thereby complementing our repertoire analysis. Using the Patent and Literature Antibody Database (PLAbDab), we searched for antibody sequences using "neuraminidase" as a keyword and identified 168 paired antibody sequences derived from 24 different sources. Through manual curation, we identified two antibodies (CR12042 and CR12044) with a centrally positioned DR motif in the CDR H3, both of which were reported in a single patent (Fig. 6a). In addition, we identified three more antibodies (AF9C, Z1A11, and Z2C2) from the study that also reported Z2B3, one of the DR motif antibodies included in our structural comparison (Fig. 4f). While CR12042 and CR12044 are described as human-derived antibodies, no details were provided regarding their source or method of isolation. CR12042 and CR12044 bound to multiple N1 NAs and showed weak binding to an N2 NA. Since they exhibited NI activity in a small molecule-based assay, we considered it likely that they target the NA active site. AF9C was isolated from an adult who received the 2014/15 Northern Hemisphere trivalent influenza vaccine (TIV), whereas Z1A11 and Z2C2 were isolated from a child who experienced a mild H7N9 infection in 2013, the same individual from whom Z2B3 had previously been isolated. AF9C was N1-specific, while Z1A11 and Z2C2 were cross-reactive to N1 and N9 NAs, similar to Z2B3. Their NI activity was observed in ELLA, but was not assessed in a small molecule-based assay, leaving it unclear whether they directly target the NA active site. All five antibodies possessed a centrally located DR motif in the CDR H3 (Fig. 6a), and except for CR12042, which has an 18-residue CDR H3, they met the search criteria used for our precursor frequency analysis (Fig. 5c), which required a CDR H3 of 19-30 residues flanked by at least eight residues on either side of the DR motif. These five antibodies were expressed as IgGs, with AF9C, Z1A11, and Z2C2 produced in germline-reverted form (GL), as only gene usage and the CDR H3 and CDR L3 sequences were available. To evaluate their binding activity, we measured binding to CA09 N1 sNAp by BLI. Four of the five antibodies showed binding, with Z2C2-GL as the exception, possibly due to reduced affinity in its germline-reverted form lacking somatic mutations that may be required for stable interaction (Fig. 6b). To investigate whether the DR motifs in these antibodies mediate receptor mimicry in a structurally conserved manner, we determined cryo-EM structures of their complexes with CA09 N1 sNAp at resolutions ranging from 2.48 to 2.76 A (Fig. 6c and Supplementary Fig. 11). All four antibodies targeted and blocked the NA active site, despite exhibiting distinct angles of approach (Fig. 6c). Remarkably, all DR motifs in these four antibodies were structurally conserved and engaged active site residues through receptor mimicry in a manner similar to the DR motif antibodies described earlier in this study (DA03E17, FNI9, 1G05, Z2B3) (Figs. 4 and 6d). These results further support the idea that receptor mimicry mediated by conserved DR motifs is a recurring strategy among NA active site-targeting antibodies.

We next investigated whether these eight DR motif antibodies share additional structural similarities beyond the DR motif. Although these antibodies exhibit diverse binding orientations to the NA active site (Fig. 6e), Z2B3 and AF9C-GL engage the active site with similar angles of approach (Supplementary Fig. 12). Both antibodies are derived from the IGHV1-69*01 germline gene, but their binding angles are slightly offset, and no notable structural similarities were observed at the level of detailed interactions, with their light chains also originating from different germline genes (Z2B3 from IGLV2-14*01 and AF9C from IGKV1-9*01). FNI9, CR12042, and CR12044 were also derived from, or predicted to originate from, the IGHV1-69 germline gene (Figs. 5a and 6a). Although FNI9 and CR12042 approached the NA active site with similar Fv angles, the orientations of their heavy and light chains were reversed (Supplementary Fig. 12). CR12044 also bound with a distinct orientation. Thus, aside from the relatively frequent use of IGHV1-69, no major structural similarities were observed among these antibodies. Nevertheless, one notable commonality was the relatively frequent usage of the IGHJ6 gene. DA03E17, 1G05, Z2B3, CR12042, AF9C, Z1A11, and even Z2C2, for which structural determination was not achieved due to loss of binding, all utilized IGHJ6 (Figs. 5a and 6a). The IGHJ6 gene is the longest among human IGHJ gene segments, and its increased usage has been observed among antibodies with long CDR H3 loops. This may contribute to the maturation of antibodies capable of reaching into the deep NA active site pocket (Fig. 6f), thereby potentially facilitating the evolution of DR motif-bearing antibodies that mediate receptor mimicry. Together, these findings expand the set of known DR motif antibodies, providing additional evidence for the structural and mechanistic convergence of this antibody class and highlighting its potential as a target for NA-based universal influenza vaccine.
Discussion

While over 5000 human mAbs targeting HA have been identified, far fewer antibodies have been characterized for NA. This imbalance underscores the need to continue isolating and studying NA-specific antibodies to better understand the immune response to NA and identify broadly protective epitopes. Such efforts will reveal common molecular features of NA antibody responses that can inform the development of universal vaccines. In this study, we provide a detailed structural and functional analysis of DA03E17, a broadly protective human mAb that targets the NA active site. Using cryo-EM, we determined the structures of DA03E17 bound to NAs from influenza A (H1N1, H3N2) and B viruses, revealing that DA03E17 inhibits the sialidase activity of NA by blocking the highly conserved active site through receptor mimicry using the conserved DR motif in CDR H3. The NA active site is highly conserved, and NA inhibition activity causes arrest of progeny virus egress from the host cell surface, preventing spread. Conserved receptor mimicry strategies employed by several NA active site-targeting antibodies likely drive a key mechanism through which broadly protective antibodies inhibit viral spread. Therefore, eliciting antibodies via vaccination that target the NA active site through receptor mimicry holds strong potential for providing broad protection against diverse influenza strains.

DA03E17 retains its binding capacity even in the presence of oseltamivir-resistant mutations, particularly in N1 and N2 subtypes, further demonstrating its robust and broad reactivity. Furthermore, DA03E17 also binds to the NA of the bovine HPAI H5N1 virus currently spreading in U.S. dairy cattle and being transmitted to other mammals, including humans. Considering its nanomolar binding affinity to this bovine H5N1 NA, along with its in vivo protective efficacy against the typical avian H5N1 virus (A/Vietnam/1203/2004) isolated from a human, as demonstrated in our previous study, DA03E17 could also serve as a valuable therapeutic option if this virus were to spread more widely in humans.

The ongoing evolution of H3N2 strains and the growing challenge of matching vaccines to circulating viruses highlight the need for broadly protective antibodies that remain effective against these evolving strains. Our cryo-EM structural analysis and MD simulations revealed that DA03E17 accommodates the N245 glycan of drifted H3N2 viruses by inducing conformational changes in the glycan. Similarly, 1G01 also induces conformational changes in the glycan itself, while FNI9 induces additional structural rearrangements in the NA loop to accommodate the N245 glycan. These differences suggest that DA03E17 and 1G01 engage the N245 glycan with minimal perturbation to the NA loop, representing an alternative mode of accommodation distinct from that of FNI9. The ability of these antibodies to structurally accommodate the N245 glycan of drifted H3N2 viruses may be of particular relevance, as H3N2-dominated influenza seasons are often associated with greater disease burden and higher hospitalization rates, especially in vulnerable populations. While these structural observations highlight varying modes of glycan engagement, further experimental data would be needed to determine whether these differences translate into functional advantages. Despite the broad cross-reactivity of DA03E17, we observed substantially reduced binding to recent N2s such as A/Kansas/14/2017, suggesting that drifted N2s may pose a challenge for NA active site-targeting antibodies. Future strategies could include immunogen designs that focus immune responses on conserved regions of N2 or structure-guided engineering of existing antibodies to improve their compatibility with recently evolved N2 NAs.

Our structural and immunogenetic analyses suggest that long CDR H3s with the DR motif near the middle of the CDR H3 could be an important requirement for effectively targeting the NA active site. Bioinformatic analysis using ultradeep NGS data shows that potential precursors with these features are prevalent in the human antibody repertoire. Furthermore, a comparison of three specific NA antibodies that use the DR motif shows their precursor frequencies span a wide range in the human antibody repertoire, from undetectable to ~ 1 in 105. These findings highlight the importance of selecting the right targets for vaccine design if these antibodies are to be consistently elicited by vaccination. The antibodies compared here have varying angles of approach and peripheral contacts, but they all bind the active site through DR motif-mediated receptor mimicry, maintaining broad reactivities. In addition, they have diverse germline origins, with IGHJ6 being the only shared feature, indicating their potential to be broadly elicited across human populations. The accompanying manuscript by Lederhofer and Borst et al. further reinforces these findings, presenting additional human antibodies with DR motif-mediated receptor mimicry, thereby underscoring the prevalence of DR motif antibodies in humans and providing structural and functional insights through both in vitro and in vivo evaluations. Nevertheless, while the prevalence of potential precursors is promising, the ability of these precursors to mature into functional broadly protective antibodies remains to be fully understood.

In conclusion, our study emphasizes the importance of long CDR H3s with the DR motif for targeting the NA active site. The structural insights gained from DA03E17, combined with the investigation of DR motif precursors in the human antibody repertoire, provide a strong foundation for developing vaccines that can elicit broadly protective antibodies. Utilizing this molecular signature to interrogate immune responses to NA and design immunogens capable of triggering protective responses across diverse populations, therefore has the potential for mitigating future influenza outbreaks.
Methods
Expression and purification of recombinant NAs and antibodies

The NAs of the H1N1 A/California/07/2009 (CA09), H1N1 A/Brisbane/02/2018 (BB18), H5N1 A/dairy cattle/Texas/24-008749-001/2024 (TX24), H3N2 A/Perth/16/2009 (PT09), H3N2 A/Indiana/08/2011 (IN11 N2), H3N2 A/Kansas/14/2017 (KS17), H3N2 A/Hong Kong/2671/2019 (HK19), and B/Colorado/06/2017 (B/Victoria-lineage; CO17) were expressed in the mammalian expression system as previously described. Briefly, the ectodomain heads of the IAV N1 (residues 83-470 in N2 numbering), N2 (residues 83-469 in N2 numbering) NAs, and CO17 B (residues 76-466) NA were fused to an N-terminal IL2 signal peptide, a hexahistidine tag, a Strep-tag, a vasodilator-stimulated phosphoprotein (VASP) tetramerization domain, and a thrombin cleavage site. Of note, all N1 NA constructs have previously reported stabilizing mutations in the inter-protomeric interface for the closed tetrameric state (stabilized NA protein, sNAp). The CA09 N1 sNAp contains ten stabilizing mutations: I99P, Y100L, C161V, E165S, S171A, V176I, S195T, V204I, R419V, and Q412M (N2 numbering). BB18 N1 sNAp and TX24 N1 sNAp also include these ten mutations but carry an additional T131Q substitution. NA constructs were transiently expressed in Expi293F cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 37  C, shaking at 125 rpm. The secreted recombinant NA proteins were purified from culture supernatant by Ni-NTA affinity chromatography (Qiagen) followed by size exclusion chromatography using a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 column (GE Healthcare) in 1X Tris-Buffered Saline (TBS) pH 7.4. The purified NAs were quantified by optical absorbance at 280 nm, and purity and integrity were analyzed by reducing and nonreducing SDS-PAGE. For DA03E17 Fab expression in mammalian cells, the heavy and light chain variable regions of DA03E17 were cloned into the pAbVec containing the corresponding human CH1 region of human IgG1 and kappa CL region, respectively. The Fab was transiently expressed in Expi293F cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 37  C, shaking at 125 rpm. The secreted recombinant Fab was purified from culture supernatant by CaptureSelect IgG-CH1 Affinity Matrix (Thermo Fisher Scientific), followed by size exclusion chromatography using a Superdex 200 Increase 10/300 column (GE Healthcare) in 1X Tris-Buffered Saline (TBS) pH 7.4.
ELISA

To evaluate the binding of mAbs, 96-well ELISA plates (PerkinElmer) were coated overnight at 4  C with 2 microg/ml of recombinant NA proteins. Plates were washed three times with a PBS solution containing 0.05% Tween-20 (PBS-T) and then blocked with 5% Non-fat milk (RPI M17200-500.0) in PBS-T. The plates were incubated for 1 h at room temperature and then washed three times with PBS-T. In the meantime, mAbs were diluted in PBS-T, starting at a concentration of 100 microg/ml with a threefold serial dilution, and then added to the plate for 1 hour at room temperature. After washing, HRP-conjugated goat anti-human IgG Fc secondary antibody (Southern Biotech) was added at a dilution of 1:20,000 in PBS-T and incubated for an additional hour at room temperature. Plates were washed three times with PBS-T and then developed with TMB substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The reaction was stopped by the addition of 2 N H2SO4, and absorbance was measured at 450 nm. The data is shown as one representative biological replicate with the mean +- SD for one ELISA experiment. The ELISAs were repeated 2 times.
ELLA

96-well high-binding plates (SpectraPlate-96HB) were coated with 100 microL per well of 25 microg/mL fetuin (Sigma #3385) diluted in coating buffer (KPL #50-84-01). Coated plates were stored at 4  C for up to two months before use. To determine the optimal concentration of recombinant NA for the assay, 50 microL of serially diluted recombinant NA (starting from 20 microg/mL with 1:3 dilutions) in sample diluent (PBS supplemented with CaCl2 and MgCl2, 1% BSA, and 0.5% Tween-20) was added to the fetuin-coated plates after three washes with PBS-T. Plates were sealed and incubated either at 37  C for 16-18 h or at 33  C for 6 h. After incubation, plates were washed five times with PBS-T and incubated with 100 microL of 1 microg/mL peanut agglutinin (PNA)-HRP (Sigma #7759-1 mg) diluted in sample diluent without Tween-20 for 2 h at room temperature. Plates were washed three times with PBS-T, and color development was performed using TMB substrate (Seracare #5120-0047). Data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism (version 10), and the linear portion of the NA titration curve was used to determine the concentration yielding a near-maximal OD450 signal (at least 10-fold over background), which was used in subsequent inhibition assays. To assess NA inhibition, antibodies were serially diluted (1:2, starting from 20 or 30 microg/mL) in sample diluent and mixed 1:1 with recombinant NA at the predetermined working concentration. A total of 50 microL of the antibody-NA mixture was added to each well of washed fetuin-coated plates. The remaining assay steps were performed as described above. Percent inhibition was calculated as: 100 - (sample OD450 / NA-only OD450 x 100), where the NA-only control (no antibody) represented 0% inhibition. Midpoint inhibitory titers (IC50) were determined using GraphPad Prism. All measurements were performed in duplicate.

passages.text: Biolayer interferometry (BLI)

Antibody affinities were determined by biolayer interferometry using an Octet Red96 (Sartorius). HIS1K biosensors (Sartorius) were hydrated in kinetics buffer (1 x PBS, pH 7.4, and 0.002% Tween 20) prior to use. Recombinant NA proteins (10 microg/ml) in kinetics buffer were immobilized on hydrated HIS1K biosensors for 300 sec through their hexahistidine tag at their N-termini, and baseline was measured in kinetics buffer for 120 sec. Following baseline measurements, the sensors were loaded with DA03E17 IgG or Fab (3-fold serially diluted from 450 nM or 2400 nM, respectively), and association and dissociation was measured for 300 and 600 sec, respectively. All assay steps were performed at 30  C with agitation set at 1000 rpm. Baseline correction was carried out by subtracting the measurements recorded for a sensor loaded with the corresponding NA in the same buffer with no Fab. The data were analyzed using the Octet-Red96 software, and the association and dissociation rates were calculated using a 1:1 model with global curve fitting.
Cryo-EM sample preparation and data collection

For each DA03E17 Fab complex with CA09 N1, KS17 N2, and CO17 B NAs, DA03E17 Fab was added at a 1:3 molar ratio of NA protomer to Fab and incubated at room temperature for 1 h before grid preparation. For the 1G01 IgG-KS17 N2 NA and FNI9 IgG-KS17 N2 NA complexes, each IgG was added at a 1:1 molar ratio of NA tetramer to IgG and incubated at room temperature for 1 h before grid preparation. For the additional DR motif NA antibodies shown in Fig. 6 (CR10242, CR12044, AF9C-GL, and Z1A11-GL), each IgG was added at a 1:2 molar ratio of NA tetramer to IgG and incubated at room temperature for 1 h before grid preparation. Final protein concentrations were between 0.4-0.5 mg/ml. For DA03E17-NA complexes, samples were mixed with octyl-beta-glucoside (OBG; final concentration 0.1% w/v) detergent to aid in particle tumbling and applied to Quantifoil 1.2/1.3 300 mesh copper grids. The grids were plunge-frozen using a Vitrobot Mark IV (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with a blot force of 1 and a blot time of 3.5-5 sec at 100% humidity and 4  C. For 1G01-KS17 N2 NA and FNI9-KS17 N2 NA complexes, samples were also mixed with OBG detergent but applied to Quantifoil 2/1 400 mesh copper and UltrAuFoil 1.2/1.3 300 mesh gold grids. The grids were plunge-frozen at room temperature with 100% humidity, a blot force of 1, and a blot time of 3.5-4.5 sec. For CR10242, CR12044, AF9C-GL, and Z1A11-GL complexes, samples were mixed with OBG detergent and applied to UltrAuFoil 1.2/1.3 300 mesh gold grids. The grids were plunge-frozen at room temperature with 100% humidity, a blot force of 1, and a blot time of 2-3 sec. All datasets were collected on a 200 kV Glacios (Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with a Falcon IV direct electron detector. Automated data collection was carried out using EPU (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at a nominal magnification of 190,000 x and a pixel size of 0.725 A, with an approximate exposure dose of 45 e-/A2 and a nominal defocus range of - 0.7 to - 1.4 mum. For each dataset, between 1684 and 6416 movie micrographs were collected. For the DA03E17 Fab + KS17 N2 NA dataset, two rounds of data collection resulted in 3166 and 3700 movie micrographs, which were combined for processing.
Cryo-EM data processing

All datasets were processed using cryoSPARC. Dose-weighted movie frame alignment was carried out using Patch motion correction in cryoSPARC live to account for stage drift and beam-induced motion. The contrast transfer function (CTF) was estimated using Patch CTF in cryoSPARC live. Micrographs were curated based on CTF fits, with those worse than 6-8 A excluded due to poor quality. Individual particles were selected from an initial subset of several hundred micrographs using Blob picker. After several rounds of 2D classification, classes resembling the Fab-NA complex were used to template pick for all micrographs. Clean particle stacks were selected through multiple rounds of 2D classification and used to generate a reference volume via ab initio reconstruction, which was then utilized as an initial volume for homogeneous refinement and/or non-uniform refinement. For the DA03E17-CA09 N1 sNAp and DA03E17-KS17 N2 NA datasets, Fab-NA complex particles underwent 3D classification. The best 3D classes were refined using either local refinement with a Fab-NA mask (DA03E17-CA09 N1) or non-uniform refinement (DA03E17-KS17 N2). Final maps were generated after global CTF refinement and application of C4 symmetry. For the apo-KS17 N2 NA, only NA particles without visible Fab binding were selected through multiple rounds of 2D classification, followed by non-uniform refinement with C4 symmetry applied and global CTF refinement, yielding the final map. For the DA03E17-CO17 B NA dataset, Fab-NA complex particles were subjected to homogeneous refinement with C4 symmetry applied, followed by global CTF refinement to generate the final map. For the 1G01-KS17 N2 NA dataset, particles selected after 2D classification were subjected to heterogeneous refinement. The best 3D classes were refined using local refinement with a Fab-NA mask and C4 symmetry applied, yielding the final map. For the FNI9-KS17 N2 NA dataset, particles selected after 2D classification were subjected to ab initio reconstruction with five classes. Particles from the highest-quality classes were then used for homogeneous refinement and local refinement with a Fab-NA mask, with no symmetry applied, yielding the final map.
Cryo-EM model building and refinement

For model building, the structures of CA09 N1 NA (PDB: 6Q23), HK19 N2 NA (PDB: 8G3O), and PK13 B NA (PDB: 6V4N) were used as the initial models for CA09 N1 sNAp, KS17 N2 NA, and CO17 B NA, respectively. The DA03E17 Fv model was generated using ABodyBuilder2. The models were fitted into the cryo-EM maps using UCSF ChimeraX. The models were manually adjusted using Coot and further refined through Rosetta Relax and real-space refinement in Phenix. N1 and N2 NAs were numbered according to the N2 numbering scheme, while the antibody Fv was numbered based on the Kabat numbering scheme. Epitope and paratope residues, as well as their interactions, were identified by using the PISA server with buried surface area (BSA > 5 A2) as the criterion. Structural figures were prepared using UCSF ChimeraX.
NA Sequence conservation analysis

For Supplementary Table 2, NA sequences for IAV Group 1 (N1, N4, N5, and N8), Group 2 (N2, N3, N6, N7, and N9), and IBV (Victoria and Yamagata) were retrieved from GISAID. Sequences for each subtype were aligned using GENETYX ver13, and SNP analysis was conducted using the BV-BRC platform (https://www.bv-brc.org/). For Fig. 2, full-length NA protein sequences from human IAV H1N1, H3N2, and IBV B/Victoria- and B/Yamagata-lineage viruses circulating from 1977 to 2023 (H1N1), 1968 to 2023 (H3N2), 1987 to 2023 (B/Victoria), and 1988 to 2020 (B/Yamagata) were downloaded from GISAID. To avoid temporal sampling bias, we sampled at most 10 sequences per year, resulting in a total of 340, 421, 278, and 251 sequences for N1, N2, B/Victoria, and B/Yamagata NAs, respectively. Multiple sequence alignments were performed using Clustal Omega, and the reference sequences used for alignment were H1N1 A/California/04/2009, H3N2 A/Kansas/14/2017, and B/Colorado/06/2017. Sequence logos were generated using WebLogo 3 and manually curated in Adobe Illustrator. For Supplementary Fig. 7, we additionally analyzed animal-origin IAV N1 and N2 NA sequences derived from HxN1 and HxN2 viruses that have circulated in avian and mammalian hosts between 1977 and 2023. A total of 432 N1 and 404 N2 sequences were included. Representative subtypes included H1N1, H5N1, and H6N1 for N1, and H1N2, H2N2, H3N2, H4N2, H5N2, H6N2, H7N2, H9N2, H11N2, and H13N2 for N2. Epitope residues in all analyses were defined based on structural contacts observed in the DA03E17-CA09 N1 NA, DA03E17-KS17 N2 NA, and DA03E17-CO17 B NA complexes.
Molecular dynamics

As starting models for our MD simulations, the cryo-EM structures of DA03E17-KS17 N2 NA (this study) and apo-KS17 N2 NA (this study) were used. The starting structures for our simulations were prepared in Molecular Operating Environment (MOE, CCG) using the Protonate3D tool. To neutralize the charges, the uniform background charge was applied, which is required to compute long-range electrostatic interactions. Using the tleap tool of the AmberTools22 package, the structures were soaked in cubic water boxes of TIP3P water molecules with a minimum wall distance of 12 A to the protein. For all simulations, parameters of the AMBER force field 19SB were used. For the glycans, we used the most recent GLYCAM force field, namely the GLYCAM-06j parameter set. We then performed 3 repetitions of 1 micros of classical molecular dynamics simulations for each system. Molecular dynamics simulations were performed in an NpT ensemble using pmemd.cuda. Bonds involving hydrogen atoms were restrained by applying the SHAKE algorithm allowing a time step of 2 fs. The Langevin thermostat was used to maintain the temperature during simulations at 300 K with a collision frequency of 2 ps-1 and a Monte Carlo barostat with one volume change attempt per 100 steps. Clustering analysis has been performed using the hierarchical average linkage clustering implement in cpptraj, by aligning on the Calpha-positions of the NA and clustering on the glycans using a RMSD distance cut-off criterion of 2.5 A.
Antibody precursor frequency estimates

Precursor searching and frequency estimates of NA active site-targeting antibodies with receptor mimicry were performed using methods described previously. The precursor definition for the first search strategy had two requirements: (1) CDR H3 length ranging from 19 to 30 amino acids, and (2) the DR motif occurred approximately in the middle of the CDR H3, >= 8 amino acids on either side. These criteria were based on the CDR H3 length and DR motif position in several NA active site-targeting antibodies. These definitions allowed for precursors with long CDR H3s possessing a DR motif, regardless of germline gene usage, with diverse V-D and D-J junctions. A total of 1.1 x 109 BCR heavy chain sequences were searched in a ultra-deep NGS dataset of 14 human donors. For the second strategy, we searched for precursors to three antibodies (DA03E17, 1G05, and Z2B3) using the following criteria: (1) CDR H3 length >= the target NA antibody. (2) D gene in the same reading frame as the NA antibody and matching the regular expression shown in Fig. 5e. (3) The D gene is flanked by the same number or more amino acids compared to the target NA antibody. (4) The DR motif is at the same position relative to the D gene as in the target NA antibody. The following D genes were used as search criteria: DA03E17 (D3-10), 1G05 (D5-12), and Z2B3 (D5-18/D5-5). While both 1G05 and Z2B3 are predicted to use D5-18, they use two different alleles (D5-18*01 and D5-18*02), which have substantially different nucleotide sequences. Also, D5-18*02 is only different from D5-12 by one nucleotide. Because D5-18*02 was not in our NGS dataset, we searched for 1G05 precursors using D5-12 instead. For Z2B3 precursors, we searched using both D5-18*01 and D5-5, as these D genes are identical.

passages.text: Decoding metabolic trade-offs in Halomonas elongata: Chemostat-based flux remodeling for industrial ectoine biosynthesis

Halomonas elongata, a moderately halophilic gamma-proteobacterium of industrial interest, serves as a microbial cell factory for ectoine:a high-value compatible solute extensively utilized in biopharmaceuticals and cosmetics. While its ectoine biosynthesis potential is well-documented, the systemic metabolic adaptations underlying osmoadaptation remain poorly characterized, limiting rational engineering strategies for optimized production. To address this gap, we employed chemostat cultivation coupled with multi-omics integration (physiological profiling, metabolomics, and metabolic flux analysis) to dissect salt-dependent metabolic network rewiring in the model strain DSM 2581T under moderate (6.0 % NaCl) and high salinity (13.0 % NaCl). Results demonstrated that, under moderate salt conditions, a specific growth rate (mu) of 0.20 h-1 significantly enhanced the ectoine-specific production rate (qp), intracellular ectoine content (pectoine), and yield coefficient (Yp/s), concurrent with redirection of carbon flux toward the Entner-Doudoroff (ED) pathway and ectoine biosynthesis. Under high salt conditions, flux through both the ED pathway and ectoine biosynthesis was further upregulated, whereas fluxes through the pentose phosphate (PP) pathway, tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, and CO2 generation were downregulated. Simultaneously, suppression of the flux from malate to pyruvate enhanced oxaloacetate synthesis, thereby increasing the supply of key precursors including glutamate, aspartate, and NADPH to fuel ectoine biosynthesis. Stepwise salt reduction experiments revealed bidirectional metabolic flexibility: elevated salinity prioritized carbon investment into ED-driven ectoine production, whereas hypo-osmotic conditions reactivate respiratory activity and the TCA cycle to fuel energy metabolism. These findings establish H. elongata as a paradigm of dynamic flux rewiring, where carbon economy is strategically reallocated between stress-protective solute biosynthesis and energy homeostasis. This study bridges the knowledge gap in understanding the physiological characteristics of H. elongata and provides a foundation for improving ectoine production and engineering strains through metabolic optimization.
Introduction

Halophilic microorganisms, thriving in hypersaline environments, have emerged as potential candidates for industrial biotechnology due to their unique metabolic resilience and sustainable bioproduction capacity under extreme conditions. These extremophiles, particularly Halomonas species, have garnered significant attention on account of their exceptional tolerance to hypersalinity, intrinsic contamination resistance, and ability to synthesize high-value bioproducts such as polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) and compatible solutes like ectoine. The strategic concept of employing halophiles as chassis organisms for next-generation industrial biotechnology (NGIB) was first validated through pioneering research demonstrating the feasibility of Halomonas bluephagenesis for large-scale fermentation under open, non-sterile conditions. This technological paradigm shift highlights the industrial advantages of halophilic systems, particularly their ability to minimize microbial contamination risks, reduce energy-intensive sterilization requirements, and facilitate continuous bioproduction processes in cost-effective open environments.

The Halomonas genus, comprising over 100 species, exhibits remarkable metabolic versatility, making it a prime candidate for diverse biotechnological applications. Members of this genus have been engineered for producing biopolymers, enzymes, amino acids, and organic acids, as well as for environmental remediation. For instance, H. campaniensis and H. boliviensis have been optimized for PHA production under high salinity, while H. elongata has been extensively studied for its ectoine biosynthesis capabilities. Ectoine, a high-value compatible solute, is widely utilized in cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, and protein stabilization due to its exceptional osmoprotective properties. H. elongata DSM 2581T, in particular, serves as an industrial workhorse for ectoine production, leveraging its ability to accumulate intracellular ectoine under hypersaline stress. Despite its biotechnological relevance, systematic investigations into its metabolic plasticity:particularly carbon flux dynamics under varying salinity:remain limited, hindering rational engineering strategies.

Recent advances in systems biology and metabolic modeling have begun to unravel the metabolic networks of halophiles. Genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs), such as the iEB1239 for H. elongata 153B, have elucidated key pathways for ectoine and PHA synthesis, revealing trade-offs between energy metabolism and osmolyte production. These models provide valuable insights into the metabolic strategies employed by halophiles to cope with high-salinity environments, including the role of the Entner-Doudoroff (ED) pathway in glucose catabolism and the importance of anaplerotic reactions for precursor supply. However, these models often lack the resolution required to in capture dynamic flux redistributions under physiological conditions. For example, while the ED pathway is known to dominate glucose catabolism in Halomonas spp., its coordination with precursor supply (e.g., oxaloacetate, glutamate) and redox balancing under osmotic stress remains poorly characterized. Studies on Chromohalobacter salexigens and H. bluephagenesis suggest salinity-dependent metabolic shifts, yet similar mechanistic insights for H. elongata are scarce.

This knowledge gap is critical: ectoine biosynthesis in H. elongata is highly growth-coupled and energy-intensive, requiring precise modulation of central carbon metabolism to optimize precursor availability. The biosynthesis of ectoine from aspartate involves multiple enzymatic steps, each requiring significant amounts of ATP, NADPH, and key precursors such as glutamate and oxaloacetate. Under high salinity, the demand for ectoine increases, placing additional strain on the cell's metabolic resources. Although advanced genetic tools, such as CRISPR-Cas9 systems, and dynamic regulatory circuits have been developed for engineering Halomonas species, the absence of a systems-level understanding of H. elongata's metabolic rewiring under salinity gradients limits strain optimization. For instance, flux balance analyses (FBA) predict suppressed TCA cycle activity during ectoine biosynthesis, but experimental validation of carbon partitioning between the ED pathway, pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), and ectoine anabolism under controlled chemostat conditions is lacking.

To address these limitations, we employed an integrated systems biology approach, combining chemostat cultivation, metabolomics, and metabolic flux analysis (MFA), to dissect salinity-driven metabolic adaptations in H. elongata DSM 2581T. Chemostat cultivation provides a controlled environment to study microbial physiology under steady-state conditions, enabling precise manipulation of growth rates and nutrient availability. By coupling this with metabolomics and MFA, we can quantify intracellular metabolite pools and flux distributions, offering a comprehensive view of metabolic rewiring under osmotic stress. Our findings show that H. elongata reprograms its carbon metabolism in response to salinity. Under high salinity (13 % NaCl), carbon flux shifts from the PPP and TCA cycle to the ED pathway and ectoine biosynthesis, enhancing precursor supply while suppressing energy-generating pathways. This is accompanied by increased oxaloacetate synthesis via phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase (PEPC) upregulation and inhibition of malate decarboxylation. Stepwise salt reduction experiments reveal H. elongata's metabolic flexibility, toggling between ectoine biosynthesis and energy homeostasis. As salinity decreases, carbon flux returns to the PPP and TCA cycle, restoring energy metabolism and reducing ectoine production. In conclusion, this study highlights the regulatory effects of salinity on H. elongata metabolism, providing a metabolic blueprint for engineering halophiles as efficient cell factories. By bridging the gap between systems biology and metabolic engineering, we pave the way for the development of robust, high-performance microbial chassis for sustainable bioproduction.
Materials and methods
Strain, media, and culture conditions
The Halomonas elongata DSM 2581T strain, a Gram-negative bacterium, employed in this research was supplied by the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Microbiology.

The activation medium consisted of the following components (g/L): peptone 10.0, yeast extract 5.0, sodium chloride 80.0, and agar 16.0. The seed medium and fermenter medium were prepared using the HE9 synthetic medium designed for H. elongata. The composition (g/L) included: sodium chloride (as per experimental conditions), potassium chloride 3.0, ammonium chloride 2.0, ammonium sulfate 2.0, sodium sulfate 2.5, magnesium sulfate heptahydrate 3.075, zinc sulfate heptahydrate 0.25, manganese sulfate monohydrate 0.09, disodium hydrogen phosphate dodecahydrate 5.0, glucose 30.0, PTM1 1 mL/L, and antifoam agent 0.05 %. The pH of all media was adjusted to 6.9 +- 0.1 using a 2 M NaOH solution. Moreover, the glucose concentration in the feed medium was 20.0 g/L, with the remaining components being the same as in the fermentation medium.

The strain was first activated on a plate containing 30 mL of activation medium. The seed culture was then grown in a 500 mL shake flask with a working volume of 100 mL. It was inoculated by rinsing the well-grown plates with 10 mL of sterile 8 % NaCl solution. The seed medium was subsequently incubated at 37  C and 200 rpm for 20 h.
Chemostat culture

We first developed an optimized chemostat culture system for H. elongata (Fig. S1), with detailed batch fermentation protocols available in our previous publication. During batch fermentation, samples were taken every hour to measure cell biomass, and when the culture entered the logarithmic phase, it was switched to chemostat culture. The peristaltic pumps for feeding and discharge were activated, and the pump speed was set according to the dilution rate (D, h-1) to maintain the discharge pump rate consistently higher than the feed rate. Samples were taken at each elution volume, with three consecutive samples collected to measure cell concentration and residual sugar. The cells were stored in a -20  C freezer for later determination of the ectoine content. The chemostat culture was deemed to have reached steady state when key physiological parameters, including carbon dioxide evolution rate (CER), oxygen uptake rate (OUR), cell biomass concentration, and residual substrate levels, maintained consistent values (+-5 % variation) across three consecutive sampling intervals.

Additionally, this study selected two salt concentrations, moderate salt (6 %, w/v) and high salt (13 %, w/v), for the experiments. Kinetic analysis of H. elongata growth dynamics in HE9 synthetic medium under 6 % NaCl condition demonstrated a maximum specific growth rate (mumax) of 0.41 h-1, as determined through nonlinear regression modeling of batch fermentation data (Fig. S1B) following established protocols. Based on these results, six dilution rates (0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30, and 0.35 h-1) were selected for experiments at a 6 % salt concentration, while three dilution rates (0.10, 0.20, and 0.30 h-1) were chosen for the 13 % salt concentration. This yielded a total of nine experimental groups, each conducted in triplicate.

Experimental design for dynamic reduction of salt concentration

To explore the physiological and metabolic responses of H. elongata to fluctuating salt concentrations, a dynamic salt reduction experiment was conducted. At a dilution rate of 0.10 h-1, after the fifth elution volume, the feed medium was switched between a high-salt concentration (13 %) and a low-salt concentration (2 %). The salt concentration does not change linearly. In this study, a theoretical model for the salt concentration over time was derived based on a black-box model, as shown in Fig. S3. C and V represent the salt concentration and volume in the bioreactor, respectively. C0 represents the initial salt concentration in the bioreactor.

In this study, a dynamic salt concentration experiment was conducted at D = 0.10 h-1, transitioning from a salt concentration of 13 %-2 %. The specific process involved maintaining a chemostat culture at 13 % salt concentration with D = 0.10 h-1. After reaching steady state, the feed medium was switched to one with a 2 % salt concentration. Based on the theoretical changes in salt concentration, sampling and intracellular metabolite measurements were conducted when the salt concentration decreased to 108 g/L, 78 g/L, 60 g/L, 40 g/L, 30 g/L, and 21 g/L, including a total of seven sampling points with the initial point. The theoretical change curve is shown in Fig. S3. Construction of the central carbon metabolism and ectoine biosynthesis network in H. elongata

Based on the reported literature and the genome annotation results from previous studies, a metabolic network model for the biosynthesis of ectoine in H. elongata was constructed. This model includes the EMP pathway, ED pathway, PP pathway, the OAA-PEP-PYR-MAL metabolic node, amino acid biosynthesis pathways, and the ectoine biosynthesis pathway (Fig. S4). Detailed information on the specific reactions within the metabolic network can be found in Table S1.

It is important to note that several assumptions and simplifications were made during the construction of the metabolic network: it was assumed that the cellular composition remains consistent across different dilution rates when the chemostat culture reaches steady state; metabolic reactions without branching were combined into a single reaction; only the main metabolites were listed in the reactions, and energy and coenzyme molecules were not included.

The EMP pathway consists of seven reactions, r1-r7, with r2 representing the conversion between G6P and F6P. Literature suggests that H. elongata likely employs the ED pathway for glucose metabolism, with the reaction's direction pending future confirmation. The ED pathway includes reactions r16 and r17. The PP pathway consists of seven reactions, r9-r15. The TCA cycle includes ten reactions, r18-r27, with r22 representing the glyoxylate cycle. The ectoine biosynthesis pathway includes the r34 reaction, converting OAA to Asp, and the simplified r49 reaction, converting Asp to ectoine. Additionally, the network includes the decarboxylation reaction r29, which converts malate to pyruvate, and the anaplerotic reaction r28, where phosphoenolpyruvate is carboxylated to form oxaloacetate. The genome annotation did not reveal the presence of the gene encoding pyruvate carboxylase, which catalyzes the direct conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate, so this reaction was not included in the metabolic network. Furthermore, the amino acid synthesis pathway includes 14 reactions, r35-r48.
Metabolic flux analysis

Metabolic flux analysis was conducted based on metabolite balances, biochemical constraints, and pseudo-steady-state assumptions for intracellular intermediate metabolites. Under these conditions, mass balance equations were established for each intermediate metabolite. The metabolic model used for analysis includes the pathways and reactions detailed in Section 2.4. The analysis incorporated the glucose consumption rate and the production rates of ectoine and carbon dioxide. The mass balance reactions in the model are represented in matrix form as S*V = b, where S is the stoichiometric matrix, V is the vector of unknown fluxes, and b is the vector corresponding to the net accumulation, input, consumption, or output of the metabolites.

The stoichiometric matrix constructed in this study comprises 59 equations, forming a 56 x 59 matrix that constitutes an over-determined system. This system was solved using the Moore-Penrose pseudo-inverse method.
Methods for intracellular metabolite analysis

For intracellular sampling, 1.2 mL of broth was taken from the bioreactor into a tube with quenching solution (-27  C, 40 % v/v methanol). A custom rapid sampling device ensured quick collection and quenching to minimize metabolite changes. Intracellular metabolites were quantified using isotope dilution mass spectrometry (IDMS), a method employed to mitigate the majority of analytical biases inherent in the measurement process.
Analytical methods

The analytical methods for determining cell dry weight, residual sugar, and ectoine content during chemostat cultivation can be found in previous publications. Specifically, after sampling from the fermenter, 10 mL of the culture broth was centrifuged in a 15 mL centrifuge tube (parameters: 12,000 rpm, 10 min). The supernatant was discarded, and the cell pellet was collected. The pellet was then resuspended in deionized water and centrifuged again under the same conditions (12,000 rpm, 10 min) to collect the cells. This washing step was repeated twice to remove the medium components (primarily sodium chloride) adhering to the cell surfaces. The resulting cells were frozen at -80  C for 30 min and subsequently lyophilized to constant weight in a freeze dryer under vacuum. The cell dry weight (CDW) was then determined.

passages.text: The physiological parameters at steady state during chemostat cultivation are shown in Fig. 1. The biomass concentration (Cx) increased initially with the dilution rate and then decreased, reaching a maximum of 12.89 +- 0.15 g/L at D = 0.25 h-1. When the dilution rate exceeded 0.25 h-1, Cx began to decline, but at higher dilution rates (0.30 and 0.35 h-1), Cx remained significantly higher than at lower dilution rates (0.10 and 0.15 h-1) (Fig. 1A). However, the substrate concentration (Cs) increased significantly when D exceeded 0.25 h-1, reaching a peak of 1.16 +- 0.06 g/L at D = 0.35 h-1 (Fig. 1C). The production of ectoine (Cp) showed a positive correlation with increasing D (Fig. 1E). Further calculations of the relevant specific rates are shown in Table 1. Both the specific oxygen uptake rate (qo2) and specific carbon dioxide production rate (qco2), as well as the specific production rate (qp) and specific substrate uptake rate (qs), increased with D, reaching 6.80 +- 0.90 and 6.74 +- 0.36 mmol/g DCW/h, 372.05 +- 9.20 mumol/g DCW/h, and 3.04 +- 0.11 mmol/g DCW/h, respectively, at D = 0.35 h-1, which were 2.58, 2.52, 5.23, and 2.71 times higher than those at D = 0.10 h-1 (Table 1). However, the respiratory quotient (RQ) values remained between 1.01 and 1.04 across different dilution rates, showing no significant differences.

Additionally, the results of the related yields showed different trends. The biomass yield based on substrate (Yx/s) exhibited an initial increase followed by stabilization. It increased with the dilution rate when D <= 0.20 h-1, but when D exceeded 0.20 h-1, Yx/s stabilized around 0.64-0.66 g/g (Fig. 1G). The specific ectoine content per unit biomass (pectoine) showed a trend of initial stability followed by a significant increase with rising D. At lower dilution rates of 0.10, 0.15, and 0.20 h-1, pectoine remained stable in the range of 0.69-0.73 mmol/g. However, when D exceeded 0.20 h-1, pectoine began to increase significantly, reaching 0.89 +- 0.03 mmol/g at D = 0.30 h-1 (Fig. 1H). Meanwhile, the ectoine yield (Yp/s) also increased to 0.10 mmol/mmol. On the other hand, the carbon dioxide yield (Yco2/s) showed an initial increase followed by a decrease as D increased. Yco2/s reached a maximum of 2.94 +- 0.07 mmol/mmol at D = 0.20 h-1, but when D exceeded 0.20 h-1, Yco2/s began to decrease significantly, dropping to 2.48 +- 0.04 mmol/mmol at D = 0.30 h-1 (Fig. 1I). Compared to the condition at D = 0.20 h-1, pectoine and Yp/s at D = 0.30 h-1 increased by 21.9 % and 25.0 %, respectively, while Yco2/s decreased by 15.6 %.

For the 13 % salt concentration, the results showed a similar trend to the 6 % condition, with higher dilution rates enhancing both biomass growth and ectoine biosynthesis. Both Cx and Cp increased with the rising dilution rate, reaching maximum values of 15.89 +- 0.36 g/L and 3.03 +- 0.03 g/L, respectively, at D = 0.30 h-1, which are 1.29 and 1.67 times higher than those at D = 0.10 h-1 (Fig. S5A and B). The specific rates (qo2, qco2, qp, and qs) showed a positive correlation with the dilution rate (Figs. S5D, E, and F). Moreover, regarding yield coefficients, Yx/s increased with increasing dilution rate. However, Yp/s and pectoine showed no significant difference between D = 0.10 and 0.20 h-1, with Yp/s being 0.11 +- 0.01 and 0.13 +- 0.01 mmol/mmol, and pectoine at 1.03 +- 0.04 and 1.05 +- 0.03 mmol/g, respectively. However, when D increased to 0.30 h-1, Yp/s and pectoine reached 0.20 +- 0.02 mmol/mmol and 1.34 +- 0.06 mmol/g, representing increases of 53.8 % and 28.8 % compared to the condition at D = 0.20 h-1. Conversely, Yco2/s at D = 0.30 h-1 was 1.83 +- 0.03 mmol/mmol, which was a significant reduction of 30.4 % compared to the condition at D = 0.10 h-1.

Further comparison of the obtained physiological parameters reveals that under the same mu condition, Cx, Cp, qp, Yp/s, and pectoine are significantly higher under the 13 % salt concentration condition compared to the 6 % salt condition (Fig. S6A and B). At the mu = 0.30 h-1, Cx, Yx/s, Cp, qp, Yp/s, and pectoine increased by 21.2 %, 24.6 %, 90.6 %, 50.5 %, 100.0 %, and 50.6 %, respectively, under 13 % salt concentration compared to the 6 % condition. However, qs showed the opposite trend, being significantly higher at 6 % salt concentration at both mu = 0.10 and 0.30 h-1. Additionally, at mu = 0.10, 0.20, and 0.30 h-1, qco2 decreased by 10.4 %, 46.7 %, and 41.2 %, respectively, under the 13.0 % salt condition compared to the 6.0 % condition. Although Yco2/S showed no significant difference at low mu (0.1 h-1) condition, it was notably lower under the 13.0 % salt condition at mu = 0.20 and 0.30 h-1 (Fig. S6D and F), with reductions of 41.5 % and 26.3 %, respectively.

Previous studies have shown that the production of ectoine by H. elongata under salt stress is highly growth-coupled, with a low proportion of by-products. Thus, the carbon intake was divided into two parts: biomass formation and carbon dioxide produced through respiration. As ectoine is an intracellular product in H. elongata, its carbon content is incorporated into the biomass during carbon balance calculations. The carbon balance under all conditions were within a reasonable range of 92 %-109 % (Table 1 and S2), indicating that the data is valid and suitable for further metabolic flux analysis.
Kinetic analysis of H. elongata in chemostat cultivation

Based on the growth kinetics model (Equation (2)), linear fitting for 1/mu and Cs were performed. As shown in Fig. 2B and F, both conditions (6 % and 13 % salt concentration) exhibit a strong linear relationship, yielding the following equations: y = 0.3319x + 2.7, R2 = 0.96 (6 % NaCl); y = 0.2085x + 2.731, R2 = 0.99 (13 % NaCl). As shown in Fig. 3, the calculated CO2 production flux was compared with the experimental data. At mu = 0.10, 0.20, and 0.30 h-1, the calculated CO2 flux values were 2.42, 2.99, and 2.46 mmol/mmol glucose, respectively, which closely matched the experimentally measured Yco2/S values of 2.41 +- 0.09, 2.94 +- 0.07, and 2.48 +- 0.04 mmol/mmol glucose, with corresponding errors of 0.5 %, 1.7 %, and 0.8 %. These results confirm the reliability of the H. elongata metabolic network model developed in this study, as well as the accuracy of its predictions. Furthermore, the data reveal a 21.7 % decrease in CO2 production flux at mu = 0.30 h-1 compared to mu = 0.20 h-1.

Furthermore, the results indicate that after glucose enters the cell, it primarily flows through the PP and ED pathways, while the second step of the EMP pathway, the flux from G6P to F6P, shows negative values. This suggests that the reversible reaction mainly flows from F6P to G6P. Additionally, the downstream flux of the EMP pathway primarily originates from the PP and ED pathways, such as the conversion of Xu5P and E4P into F6P and GA3P, and the conversion of KDPG into GA3P and PYR in the ED pathway. The relative fluxes of the two ED pathway reactions, r16 (6PG to KDPG) and r17 (KDPG to GA3P and PYR), increase with mu and reach their maximum at mu = 0.30 h-1, with values of 60.9 and 60.3 mmol/100 mmol glucose, respectively. The relative flux of the PP pathway reaches its maximum at mu = 0.20 h-1, significantly higher than the other two mu conditions. For example, the flux of r10 (6PG to Ru5P) is 56.6 mmol/100 mmol glucose at mu = 0.30 h-1, a 13.1 % decrease compared to 65.1 mmol/100 mmol glucose at mu = 0.20 h-1. However, after calculating the flux distribution at the metabolic node 6 PG, the results show that the proportion of glucose decomposed through the PP pathway initially increases and then decreases with increasing mu, peaking at 53 % under mu = 0.20 h-1. In contrast, the proportion of glucose decomposed via the ED pathway shows the opposite trend, reaching a maximum of 52 % at mu = 0.30 h-1 (Fig. S7A).

Moreover, the analysis of the TCA cycle revealed that its relative flux showed no significant differences between the conditions of mu = 0.10 and mu = 0.30 h-1 but peaked at mu = 0.20 h-1. For instance, the relative flux of r19 was 72.9 mmol/100 mmol glucose at mu = 0.20 h-1, whereas at mu = 0.10 and mu = 0.30 h-1, it decreased to 61.2 and 60.6 mmol/100 mmol glucose, corresponding to reductions of 16.1 % and 16.9 %, respectively. Similarly, the relative flux of PEP conversion to OAA was 46.5 and 45.2 mmol/100 mmol glucose under mu = 0.10 and mu = 0.20 h-1, respectively, showing minimal variation. However, this flux increased to 50.6 mmol/100 mmol glucose at mu = 0.30 h-1, representing increases of 8.8 % and 11.9 % compared to the former two conditions. Further analysis indicated that PEP carboxylation to OAA consistently exhibited a significantly higher flux than PEP conversion to PYR. The proportion of PEP flux directed toward OAA was lowest at 54.6 % under mu = 0.20 h-1 and highest at 60.4 % under mu = 0.30 h-1 (Fig. S7B). In addition, under mu = 0.30 h-1, the flux of MAL conversion to PYR was lowest at 22.0 mmol/100 mmol glucose. By contrast, this flux peaked at 33.0 mmol/100 mmol glucose under mu = 0.20 h-1, representing a reduction of 33.3 % (Fig. S7B).
The flux changes in amino acid biosynthesis and ectoine biosynthesis pathways at 6 % salt concentration

As depicted in Fig. 3, under mu = 0.10 h-1, the relative fluxes of most amino acid biosynthesis reactions were higher compared to the other two mu conditions. Notably, the relative fluxes for Glu and Asp biosynthesis were significantly greater than those of other amino acids, each exceeding 20 mmol/100 mmol glucose. This level was substantially higher than the fluxes for other amino acids, all of which remained below 5 mmol/100 mmol glucose. In the ectoine metabolic pathway, the relative flux for Asp biosynthesis, a direct precursor, reached 25.1 mmol/100 mmol glucose under mu = 0.30 h-1, marking increases of 23.6 % and 23.0 % compared to 20.3 and 20.4 mmol/100 mmol glucose under mu = 0.10 and mu = 0.20 h-1, respectively. Similarly, Glu showed an initial decline followed by an increase, peaking at 37.6 mmol/100 mmol glucose under mu = 0.30 h-1, which was 20.1 % higher than under mu = 0.20 h-1. The relative flux for ectoine biosynthesis displayed no significant difference between mu = 0.10 and mu = 0.20 h-1 but reached a maximum of 13.4 mmol/100 mmol glucose under mu = 0.30 h-1, increasing by 31.4 % and 22.9 % compared to the lower mu conditions. Conversely, the total flux of Asp toward other branched amino acids (Lys, Thr, and Met) decreased with increasing mu, reaching a minimum of 1.8 mmol/100 mmol glucose under mu = 0.30 h-1. This represented reductions of 45.5 % and 35.7 % compared to mu = 0.10 and mu = 0.20 h-1, respectively (Fig. S7C).

Intracellular metabolic fluxes under three mu conditions at 13.0 % salt concentration were calculated and compared to those at 6.0 %, as shown in Fig. 4. At 13.0 % salt concentration, nine reactions (r2, r16, r17, r35, r29, r30, r34, r42, and r49) displayed significantly higher relative fluxes than those at 6.0 %. These reactions are primarily associated with two steps of the ED pathway, PEP carboxylation to OAA, the conversion of OAA to Asp, ectoine biosynthesis, and the synthesis of amino acids such as Glu, Ala, and Val. In contrast, pathways with lower fluxes included a broader range of reactions, spanning 21 steps in the PP pathway and TCA cycle.

At mu = 0.30 h-1 condition, a direct comparison of intracellular fluxes revealed marked differences between the two salt conditions (Fig. 4B). At 13.0 % salt concentration, the ED pathway flux was substantially higher, while the PP pathway and TCA cycle fluxes were significantly lower. Averaging the relative changes across all reactions in a pathway showed that, at mu = 0.30 h-1, the ED pathway flux increased by 11.7 %, while the PP pathway and TCA cycle fluxes decreased by 23.2 % and 25.5 %, respectively. The fluxes for PEP carboxylation to OAA, OAA conversion to Asp, and ectoine biosynthesis increased by 14.4 %, 56.6 %, and 48.5 %, respectively. Furthermore, the synthesis fluxes of Glu and Ala rose by 28.7 % and 14.3 %, respectively. In contrast, CO2 biosynthesis flux decreased by 23.1 %, and MAL decarboxylation to PYR dropped sharply by 66.8 %. Moreover, the proportion of glucose metabolized via the ED pathway increased with mu, reaching 61 % at mu = 0.30 h-1, a 17.6 % rise compared to 6.0 % salt concentration (Fig. S8A). Similarly, the proportion of PEP carboxylation to OAA slightly increased, peaking at 63 %, compared to a maximum of 60 % under 6.0 % conditions (Fig. S8B). Consistent with the 6.0 % condition, the synthesis fluxes of most amino acids (e.g., Lys, Met, Thr, Gln, and His) were significantly reduced at higher mu condition (Fig. S8C). Flux estimates indicated that NADPH and NADH production fluxes at 13.0 % salt concentration were 94.4 and 352.9 mmol/100 mmol glucose, respectively, reflecting reductions of 33.6 % and 13.9 % relative to 142.1 and 409.9 mmol/100 mmol glucose at 6.0 %. Despite the significant decreases in intracellular NADH and ATP pools at 13.0 % salt concentration, the AEC value and NADPH pool remained stable (Fig. 4B).

As illustrated in Fig. 6, the physiological and metabolic states corresponding to seven sampling points were analyzed. The results demonstrate that biomass, ectoine content, and Yx/s decreased with declining salt concentration. In contrast, both qco2 and qs increased as the salt concentration decreased (Fig. 6). Specifically, qco2 increased by 75.2 % from 2.38 to 4.17 mmol/g DCW/h, and qs rose by 50.0 % from 0.92 to 1.38 mmol/g DCW/h. Additionally, qp exhibited a declining trend during the rapid decrease phase of salt concentration (130-60 g/L), followed by stabilization during the slower decrease phase (60-20 g/L). In the latter phase, qp stabilized at approximately 55 mumol/g DCW/h, showing no significant further reduction (Fig. 6G). Conversely, Yco2/S increased linearly during the rapid decline phase and stabilized in the slower phase, reaching a steady value of 3.00-3.04 mmol/mmol. At a salt concentration of 21 g/L, qp decreased by 48.5 %, while Yco2/S increased by 17.0 % compared to the initial condition at 130 g/L. Metabolic flux changes in H. elongata during dynamic reduction of salt concentration

As shown in Fig. 6J, the fluxes of four reactions in the EMP pathway decreased significantly with the dynamic reduction in salt concentration, while three reactions exhibited an increasing trend. The increasing reactions (r3, r4, and r5), involving the conversion of F6P to GA3P, were influenced by compensatory fluxes from the PP pathway. The results indicate that the fluxes of reactions in the PP pathway increased as the salt concentration decreased. Similarly, most reactions in the TCA cycle, including the glyoxylate cycle reaction (r22), also displayed increased fluxes. Moreover, the synthesis fluxes of most amino acids increased rapidly during the fast decline phase of salt concentration but slowed significantly during the slow decline phase. However, the synthesis fluxes of four amino acids, Glu, Asp, Ala, and Val (reactions r30, r34, r35, and r42), were reduced. The fluxes in the ED pathway, ectoine biosynthesis pathway, and the anaplerotic PEP carboxylation to OAA decreased gradually with the declining salt concentration, following a rapid reduction during the fast decline phase and a slower reduction in the slow decline phase.

Further analysis quantified the fluxes involving four key metabolic nodes, as shown in Fig. S10. During the rapid decline phase, the proportion of glucose catabolized via the ED pathway decreased rapidly, but the rate of decrease slowed when the salt concentration fell below 60 g/L. At 21 g/L salt concentration, the proportions of glucose catabolized through the ED and PP pathways were 43.9 % and 56.1 %, respectively, compared to 50.4 % and 49.6 % at 130 g/L, representing a change of 8.8 % (Fig. S10A). For the PEP-PYR-OAA metabolic node, during the rapid decline phase, the metabolic fluxes for PEP carboxylation to OAA and MAL-to-OAA conversion decreased sharply, while the fluxes of PEP and MAL toward PYR increased rapidly (Fig. S10B). Compared to the 130 g/L condition, the fluxes from PEP and MAL to OAA decreased by 2.6 % and 7.9 %, respectively, at 21 g/L. Additionally, the flux of Asp directed toward ectoine biosynthesis decreased rapidly and then stabilized, with a 19.2 % reduction at 21 g/L (Fig. S10C). In contrast, the flux of Asp directed toward other branched amino acid pathways (Lys, Thr, and Met) increased significantly, rising by 115.8 % at 21 g/L (Fig. S10D).
Discussion
The ED and PP pathways as the primary glucose catabolic pathways in H. elongata

In H. elongata, glucose is primarily metabolized through the PP and ED pathways, with the ED pathway playing a dominant role. Unlike terrestrial model strains such as E. coli and Bacillus subtilis, most marine bacteria, including H. elongata, predominantly utilize the ED pathway for glucose metabolism. This observation aligns with the findings of Klingner et al., who employed 13C isotope experiments to investigate glucose catabolism in marine bacteria. Similarly, Kindzierski et al. suggest that the ED pathway may be the primary glycolytic route in H. elongata, although conclusive experimental proof for its dominance in Halomonas species remains lacking. Notably, most members of the Halomonadaceae family, including H. elongata's close relative Chromohalobacter salexigens, rely on the ED pathway rather than the EMP pathway for glucose metabolism. There is no forward flux from G6P to F6P via the EMP pathway; instead, a reverse flux from F6P to G6P is observed. This suggests that the phosphohexose isomerase (EC: 5.3.1.9) responsible for this reaction exhibits low catalytic activity toward G6P, likely explaining why glucose cannot be entirely metabolized through the EMP pathway. F6P is primarily derived from the PP pathway and is largely converted back into G6P, re-entering the PP and ED pathways. The proportions of glucose catabolized through the ED and PP pathways vary with specific growth rates. At low specific growth rates (0.10 and 0.20 h-1), a larger proportion of glucose is metabolized through the PP pathway, reaching up to 53 %. Conversely, at higher specific growth rates, glucose metabolism shifts significantly toward the ED pathway, with its proportion increasing to 52 %. The metabolic flux through the ED pathway continues to rise with increasing growth rates. Unlike strains that rely exclusively on the ED pathway, H. elongata demonstrates significant metabolic flux through the downstream reactions of the EMP pathway. This is attributed to the flux returning to the EMP pathway from the PP and ED pathways, which provide critical molecules such as NADH and ATP for cell growth.

At mu = 0.20 h-1, the cell yield reaches its peak, corresponding to the highest flux through the PP pathway. The PP pathway not only supplies precursor metabolites essential for growth but also generates NADPH necessary for protein synthesis. This finding is consistent with studies on Aspergillus niger, where higher PP pathway flux correlates with high protein yields. Despite its lower energy efficiency compared to the EMP pathway:yielding only 1 mol of ATP and 1 mol of NADH per mol of glucose metabolized (or an additional 1 mol of NADPH via a phosphorylated route):the ED pathway offers distinct advantages. By producing key precursor metabolites such as PYR through shorter reaction steps, it minimizes the accumulation of intermediate products, thereby maintaining high cell conversion efficiency. The higher cell yield observed at 13 % salt concentration further supports this interpretation.
Elevated specific growth rate triggers metabolic shift in H. elongata

Under high specific growth rate conditions, H. elongata maintains a high metabolic flux for ectoine biosynthesis, while the increased flux of the ED pathway alone does not fully account for this phenomenon. The biosynthesis of 1 mol of ectoine, starting from Asp, requires the consumption of 1 mol each of ATP, NADPH, Glu, and AcCoA, indicating that five key substances, including Asp, influence ectoine biosynthesis. OAA is the primary source of Asp, and a study by Hobmeier et al. highlighted the high metabolic demand for OAA in the high-flux synthesis of ectoine, emphasizing the critical importance of an adequate OAA supply. In H. elongata, OAA is primarily generated via two pathways: one involves PEP carboxylase, which catalyzes the conversion of PEP and CO2 to OAA, while the other generates OAA from MAL in the TCA cycle. Under high mu conditions, the flux of the PEP carboxylation reaction, generating OAA, is significantly higher than under low mu conditions, which may explain the reduced CO2 yield. Simultaneously, the flux of MAL decarboxylation to PYR decreases, indicating that more MAL is being utilized for OAA production. These findings suggest that under high mu conditions, the cell's demand for OAA is markedly increased, further supported by a higher OAA metabolic pool. Moreover, under high mu conditions, the metabolic pools of NADPH, Glu, and AcCoA are significantly elevated, indicating enhanced precursor substance supply. The substantially increased qo2 and the rise in NADH metabolic pool also reflect continuous ATP supply enhancement. The elevated energy load further corroborates this conclusion. Notably, under high mu conditions, the levels of lysine (Lys), threonine (Thr), and glutamine (Gln) decrease significantly. Both Lys and Thr are part of the aspartate family and share aspartate semialdehyde as a common precursor with ectoine. Studies have shown that genetically engineered blockage of the pathway from aspartate semialdehyde to Lys significantly increases ectoine production. This suggests that the mu regulates the metabolic distribution of aspartate semialdehyde, directing more toward ectoine biosynthesis under high mu conditions, while flux to other branch amino acids is reduced.

The decline in the Gln metabolic pool occurs when the specific growth rate exceeds 0.20 h-1. Gln and Glu are the two most abundant amino acids in H. elongata, playing roles in osmoregulation and acting as important nitrogen donors in various metabolic reactions. Studies have indicated that under salt stress, the activity of glutamine synthetase (GS), which catalyzes the conversion of AKG and Gln to Glu, is significantly enhanced. Therefore, the decrease in Gln may be linked to increased GS activity, which partially converts Gln to Glu to meet the precursor requirements for ectoine synthesis, thereby further boosting product yield. In summary, at a 6.0 % salt concentration, as the specific growth rate increases, H. elongata shifts its metabolism from the PP pathway, CO2 generation, and competitive amino acid synthesis to the ED pathway, OAA metabolism, and ectoine biosynthesis.
Strict regulation of ectoine biosynthesis by salt concentration in H. elongata

At a salt concentration of 13.0 %, the intracellular metabolism of H. elongata undergoes significant changes, with increased flux through the ED pathway, PEP carboxylation to generate OAA, and OAA conversion to ectoine. Conversely, pathways such as malate to pyruvate conversion, aspartate diversion to branched amino acids, and carbon dioxide synthesis are reduced. Additionally, flux through the PP pathway and TCA cycle decreases, lowering NADPH and NADH synthesis, which increases the metabolic efficiency demands on the cell. Compared to glycolysis, the ED pathway involves fewer protein steps and a stronger thermodynamic driving force, while simplifying glucose metabolism and enabling the rapid production of PEP and PYR. This is particularly crucial for H. elongata, as the rapid production of PEP meets the metabolic requirements for OAA. Moreover, the ED pathway shares the initial step from G6P to 6PG with the PP pathway, preventing the loss of carbon equivalents through decarboxylation during NADPH production, which is vital for improving carbon conversion efficiency. The reduced flux in carbon dioxide synthesis further supports this notion. Contrary to traditional understanding, studies have shown that the ED pathway generates NADPH more efficiently than the PP pathway, which may explain why the NADPH content in H. elongata remains stable under 13.0 % salt conditions.

The dynamic salt concentration reduction experiment further demonstrated that ectoine biosynthesis is strictly regulated by salt concentration and appears to be influenced by the rate of change in salt concentration. During the experiment, the salt concentration decreased at a rapid-to-slow rate. In the rapid decline phase, both cell biomass and ectoine content rapidly decreased, while cellular respiration significantly increased. As the salt concentration entered the slow decline phase, physiological parameters stabilized, and metabolic fluxes adjusted, with increased flux through the PP pathway and TCA cycle, while flux through the ED pathway decreased. As the salt concentration decreased, glucose metabolism shifted from the ED pathway to the PP pathway. This result is consistent with steady-state experimental observations and supports findings from the halophilic bacterium C. salexigens, which showed that the flux through the ED pathway was higher under high salt conditions than under low salt conditions. In this study, the reduction in salt concentration enhanced cellular respiration and TCA cycle flux, significantly increasing the NADH metabolic pool. However, the ATP metabolic pool did not increase continuously, and after the salt concentration dropped to 60 g/L at the 10-h mark, it began to decrease. Oren's research suggested that halophilic bacteria incur higher energy costs for survival under high salt conditions, so a reduction in salt concentration decreases the energy cost for H. elongata. In the 130-60 g/L salt concentration range, the ATP pool increased gradually. However, once the salt concentration dropped to 60 g/L, ATP levels began to decrease, suggesting that reduced salt concentration may inhibit ATP synthase activity in the respiratory chain. This observation is consistent with literature, where studies showed that C. salexigens yields 2.6 times more ATP per mole of glucose under high salt conditions than under low salt conditions. , although flux through the PP pathway increased, the NADPH reducing power did not improve significantly, further supporting the hypothesis that the ED pathway is more efficient at NADPH generation.

As the salt concentration decreased, the metabolic demand for ectoine synthesis precursors, particularly OAA, diminished. This was evident in the reduced replenishment of OAA from PEP carboxylation and the enhanced decarboxylation of malate to pyruvate. These findings suggest that the metabolic demand for OAA in H. elongata is regulated not only by growth rates but also by salt concentration. Karina et al. also found that mutants lacking PEP carboxylase (Ppc) exhibited significantly restricted growth under high salt conditions. Meanwhile, to balance the accumulation of the Asp metabolic pool caused by the reduced ectoine biosynthesis pathway, aspartate was increasingly diverted to branched amino acid biosynthesis (Lys, Thr, and Met). In conclusion, the dynamic salt concentration reduction experiment validated the migration pattern of intracellular metabolic flux in response to salt concentration changes: under high salt conditions, metabolic flux is directed more towards the ED pathway, OAA metabolism, and ectoine biosynthesis, while as the salt concentration decreases, flux gradually shifts towards the PP pathway, TCA cycle, and carbon dioxide synthesis pathways.
Conclusion

This study investigated the metabolic characteristics of H. elongata and the regulation of ectoine biosynthesis under different mu and salt concentrations using chemostat cultures, combined with metabolomic and metabolic flux analyses. The results showed that, as mu increased, cellular respiration, substrate consumption, and ectoine biosynthesis all intensified. Notably, when mu exceeded 0.20 h-1, significant metabolic shifts occurred. Specifically, the flux transitioned from the PP pathway and amino acid synthesis to the ED pathway, OAA metabolism, and ectoine biosynthesis. Additionally, intracellular pools of ectoine precursors (Asp, Glu, NADPH, AcCoA) expanded to support high-throughput ectoine biosynthesis. Under high-salt conditions, these metabolic shifts were further amplified, with increased flux through the ED pathway and ectoine biosynthesis, while fluxes through the PP pathway, TCA cycle, and CO2 production were significantly reduced. Moreover, the MAL-to-PYR flux decreased, which in turn promoted OAA synthesis. Dynamic salt reduction experiments further confirmed that ectoine biosynthesis and its precursor pathways are stringently regulated by salt concentration. Overall, this study highlights the regulatory effects of both salt concentration and mu on H. elongata metabolism, providing valuable insights into its mechanisms for salt adaptation.

passages.text: Cadmium-Induced Mitochondrial and MAMs Dysregulation in Rat Testis: The Protective Role of D-Aspartate
ABSTRACT

Cadmium (Cd), a heavy metal, disrupts the structure of seminiferous tubules and induces cell death at multiple stages of sperm development. Cd also impairs Leydig cells (LCs), resulting in reduced serum testosterone (T) levels. This study primarily examined the impact of Cd on the mitochondrial compartment and mitochondrial-associated endoplasmic reticulum membranes (MAMs) in rat testis. Additionally, the potential of D-aspartate (D-Asp) to mitigate Cd-induced effects on steroidogenesis and spermatogenesis was assessed by administering D-Asp simultaneously or preventively with Cd. The findings demonstrated that Cd exerts reprotoxicity by affecting the mitochondrial compartment and MAMs, evidenced by an imbalance in mitochondrial dynamics, impaired mitophagy pathway, and downregulated mitochondrial biogenesis. Cd exposure also reduced lipid transfer-related factor expression and increased ER stress. Moreover, elevated levels of Ca2+ transfer-related proteins, indicative of perturbed Ca2+ homeostasis, may be associated with enhanced oxidative stress and apoptosis, which are known effects of Cd. Immunofluorescent analysis revealed that the Cd-induced mitochondrial and MAMs damage was prominent in LCs, spermatocytes, and spermatids, confirming the metal's adverse effects on steroidogenesis and spermatogenesis. Conversely, co-administration or preventive administration of D-Asp with Cd preserved mitochondrial homeostasis and functional ER-mitochondria interactions. In conclusion, the study offers novel insights into the cellular mechanisms underlying Cd-induced reprotoxicity. Importantly, it highlights the efficacy of D-Asp in preventing or counteracting testicular damage caused by Cd by enhancing mitochondrial and MAMs functionality.
